text.p: France's new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin brought Communists and Greens into a young, broad-left government on Wednesday, giving a major role to women as the defeated Gaullists wallowed in recrimination.

After two apparently harmonious meetings with Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, Jospin unveiled a left-wing coalition brimming with new faces born of the stunning defeat of the centre-right in last Sunday's parliamentary election.

Of 14 senior ministers, five are women with Martine Aubry, 46, daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors, taking the number two slot in charge of a superministry of employment and social security.

In a gesture of goodwill to Chirac, Jospin appointed two non-confrontational Socialists to the key foreign affairs and defence portfolios, dealing with areas in which the president has a big say under "cohabitation" power-sharing.
Hubert Vedrine, 49, a former top aide and diplomatic adviser to the late president Francois Mitterrand with long experience of managing "cohabitation", will be foreign minister.

Alain Richard, 51, a financial expert with no military expertise, was put in charge of defence, suggesting he may largely manage the huge military budget and leave Chirac and Jospin to set strategic policy.
The Communists returned to government for the first time since walking out on the Socialists in 1984.
Former railwayman Jean-Claude Gayssot took the transport portfolio his party held in the 1980s, with added responsibility for housing and public works.
His party comrade Marie-George Buffet, one of the new, female faces, becomes youth and sports minister.
Greens leader Dominique Voynet, an anti-nuclear campaigner and single mother whose ecologist party won its first seats, took the environment and regional development brief.
Jean-Pierre Chevenement, founder of the anti-Maastricht leftist Citizens' Movement, who resigned as defence minister in 1991 in protest at the Gulf War, was named interior minister.
But Socialist officials made clear that he and the Communists would have to accept the government's pro-European line in support of a single European currency.

The Communist Party has not said what, if any, assurances it had obtained on its demands. These include a higher minimum wage, a cut in value-added tax and a speedy implementation of promises to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 to reduce record 12.8 percent unemployment.

Communist leader Robert Hue told reporters: "The Communist party is fully aware of the scale of efforts that need to be accomplished and of the role it will play along with the labour and citizens' movement."
Jospin received a warm letter of congratulations from U.S. President Bill Clinton and talked with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, France's main European ally, aides said.

Chirac's own authority came under fire on the right, with a growing chorus of Gaullists demanding the immediate removal of defeated ex-prime minister Alain Juppe as leader of his RPR party and the heads of several of the president's closest aides.

Before finalising his list, Jospin reorganised his own party. Ex-premier Laurent Fabius was nominated for speaker of the new National Assembly, in which the combined left will have a 62-seat majority over the centre-right.
Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande will take over as acting party leader while first secretary Jospin is premier.
Jospin appeared to have made a success of his first test in "cohabitation", forced on Chirac following the election defeat of the outgoing centre-right coalition.

Elisabeth Guigou, 50, a cool technocrat with a strong background on European issues, was surprisingly named to the sensitive job of justice minista time when a wave of corruption probes targets all parties.

Jospin aide Pierre Moscovici was given the European affairs portfolio under Vedrine, taking over negotiations on the reform of European Union institutions just two weeks before a crucial summit in Amsterdam.

New finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn drafted the Socialist party's economic policy which includes pledges to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay.

Strauss-Kahn will have to balance aims of pushing through the reforms with no tax hikes, all the while meeting another pledge of joining a single European Union currency from 1999 without imposing further austerity.
Market economists said there were no big surprises in the government lineup but the potential for higher public spending and increased deficits should not be neglected.

"There are definitely risks in this government. You have streaks in the government which are anti-Maastricht, in favour of increased spending. These are things to to worry about," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, an economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
A first cabinet meeting will be held on Thursday at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT).
Out of office, Juppe struggled to cling to his job as Gaullist party boss as erstwhile allies sharpened their knives.
Pierre Mazeaud, a veteran Gaullist parliamentarian, blamed Juppe and top aides to Chirac for convincing him to call a snap election which backfired disastrously.
"(Chirac) must ask himself questions about his aides...It is high time to draw the conclusions from this failure, and for everyone to take the consequences," Mazeaud said.
